title: Probability at speed
objectives: Answer short probability questions at about two minutes each, without a calculator.

screens.prose: Trader batteries are reported to include a probability paper at about two minutes a question, with no calculator. Two cards are dealt from a well-shuffled 52-card deck.
screens.question: What is the chance that both cards are aces?

options.why: You used $\tfrac{4}{52}$ twice, as if the first ace went back in the deck.
That is the second card alone, given an ace came first. Multiply by $\tfrac{4}{52}$ for the first.
That is one card being an ace. Both must be.

hints.text: After an ace, how many aces and how many cards are left?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first ace leaves the deck before the second card.

byKey.rep: You used $\tfrac{4}{52}$ twice, as if the first ace went back in the deck.
byKey.second: That is the second card alone, given an ace came first. Multiply by $\tfrac{4}{52}$ for the first.
byKey.one: That is one card being an ace. Both must be.

explain.text: First an ace: $\tfrac{4}{52}$. Then 3 aces remain among 51: $\tfrac{3}{51}$. Multiply: $\tfrac{12}{2652} = \tfrac{1}{221}$.

screens.prose: Write the sample space before any sum. Each cell is one equally likely result of two dice; the number is the total. The primes up to 12 are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.
screens.question: Tap every cell whose total is prime.

hints.text: The diagonal of 7s has six cells.

feedback.correct: 15 cells: one 2, two 3s, four 5s, six 7s and two 11s.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each total against the list 2, 3, 5, 7, 11.

byKey.r3c6: 9 is $3 \times 3$, so it is not prime.
byKey.r4c5: 9 is $3 \times 3$, so it is not prime.
byKey.r5c4: 9 is $3 \times 3$, so it is not prime.
byKey.r6c3: 9 is $3 \times 3$, so it is not prime.
byKey.r1c1: A total of 2 is prime: its only factors are 1 and 2.
byKey.r5c6: A total of 11 is prime: tap both 11s.
byKey.r6c5: A total of 11 is prime: tap both 11s.

explain.text: Fifteen cells have a prime total: $1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2$. The diagonal of 7s holds six of them. Counting from the grid beats any formula here.

screens.prose: The grid you tapped is the **sample space**: every equally likely result. Count the favourable cells, divide by the total, and write the fraction in lowest terms before you read the options.
screens.question: Which option is the chance that the total is prime?

options.why: You left out the totals 2 and 11. Both are prime: 15 cells, not 12.
That is the chance the total is not prime: 21 of 36.
You treated the 11 totals as equally likely. A 7 has six cells and a 2 only one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded cells, then simplify.

byKey.third: You left out the totals 2 and 11. Both are prime: 15 cells, not 12.
byKey.comp: That is the chance the total is not prime: 21 of 36.
byKey.eleven: You treated the 11 totals as equally likely. A 7 has six cells and a 2 only one.

explain.text: 15 of the 36 cells are prime, and $\tfrac{15}{36} = \tfrac{5}{12}$. The options list only lowest terms, so simplify first. That one step saves a hunt through the options.

screens.prose: A condition affects 2% of people. A test catches 90% of cases and flags 10% of the clear by mistake. You test positive. Count people, not chances: picture 1,000.

state.caption: 1,000 people; the shaded dots have the condition

screens.question: Fill in the counts, then the chance you have the condition.

hints.text: 18 of the 20 test positive; 10% of the 980 clear is 98.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the 1,000 by the 2% first, then apply each test rate inside its group.

byKey.r2c1: False positives come only from the 980 clear: 10% of 980 is 98, not 10% of 1,000.
byKey.r3c1: Of 116 positives, 18 have it: $\tfrac{18}{116} = 0.155$. 0.9 is the reverse chance, a positive given the condition.

explain.text: Of 1,000 people, 20 have it and 18 of them test positive. Of the 980 clear, 98 test positive. So only 18 of 116 positives have it: $\tfrac{9}{58} \approx 0.155$.

screens.prose: Roll a fair die. On a 6, roll once more and add the second roll. The grid is the sample space: each cell is equally likely, and shows the total. The expected total is the mean of the cells.
screens.question: What is the expected total?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh each row’s mean by its chance and add.

byKey.no-reroll: 3.5 ignores the second roll. On a 6 you add 3.5 on average, one time in six.
byKey.always: 7 adds a second roll every time. It comes only after a 6.
byKey.six-only: 9.5 is row 6 alone. Weigh it by $\tfrac16$ and add the other rows.

explain.text: Rows 1 to 5 give $\tfrac56 \times 3 = 2.5$ and row 6 gives $\tfrac16 \times 9.5 = 1.583$. Together $\tfrac{49}{12} \approx 4.083$. A shortcut: $3.5 + \tfrac16 \times 3.5$, the same number.

screens.prose: A question asks for the chance of a total of 7 with two dice. The options are A $\tfrac76$, B $\tfrac16$, C $-\tfrac16$ and D $\tfrac56$. Some can go before any working.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which options can you cross out without working?

options.why: $\tfrac16$ lies between 0 and 1, so it stays until you work. It is in fact the answer.
$\tfrac56$ is a possible chance, so it stays until you work. It is the chance of any other total.

hints.text: Which options are above 1 or below 0? The 7s are only for checking later.
A is above 1 and C is below 0.

feedback.correct: A and C: no probability is above 1 or below 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cross out only what no probability can be.

byKey.b: $\tfrac16$ lies between 0 and 1, so it stays until you work. It is in fact the answer.
byKey.d: $\tfrac56$ is a possible chance, so it stays until you work. It is the chance of any other total.

explain.text: $\tfrac76$ is above 1 and $-\tfrac16$ is below 0, so both go at once. That leaves two options, a guess worth 0 even at +1 and −1. The grid’s diagonal of six 7s gives $\tfrac16$.

screens.prose: Two cards are dealt from a full deck. A pair means the same rank: two sevens, two queens.
screens.question: What is the chance that the two cards form a pair?

options.why: You used $\tfrac{4}{52}$ for the second card, as if the first went back. It did not: 3 of 51 match.
That is a pair of aces only. Any rank will do, so the first card can be anything.
The first card is gone, so 51 cards are left, not 52.

hints.text: The first card can be anything.
How many of the 51 cards left share its rank?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix the first card, then count matches among the cards left.

byKey.rep: You used $\tfrac{4}{52}$ for the second card, as if the first went back. It did not: 3 of 51 match.
byKey.aces: That is a pair of aces only. Any rank will do, so the first card can be anything.
byKey.den: The first card is gone, so 51 cards are left, not 52.

explain.text: The first card is free. Then 3 of the remaining 51 cards match its rank: $\tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{17}$. Using $\tfrac{4}{52}$ forgets that the first card left the deck.

screens.prose: Each time you wrote the sample space or a crowd first, counted, and only then simplified. $$P(A) = \frac{\text{favourable}}{\text{total}}, \qquad P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A).$$ Then match the options, after crossing out the impossible ones.
screens.question: Three flips of a fair coin. What is the chance all three land the same way?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the outcomes where all three match.

byKey.heads-only: $\tfrac18$ counts HHH alone. TTT is all the same too: $\tfrac28$.
byKey.half: Count the 8 outcomes: only HHH and TTT match, so $\tfrac28$.

explain.text: Of the 8 equally likely outcomes, HHH and TTT match. That is $\tfrac28 = \tfrac14$. Another route: the second and third flips must copy the first, $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12$.

screens.prose: Here is the natural-frequency method for the test from earlier. Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that takes a rate of the wrong group.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Picture 1,000 people, so every count is whole
2% have the condition: 20; the other 980 are clear

lines.why: The 10% applies to the 980 who are clear, not to everyone.

hints.text: Start with the crowd, then split it.
The two test rates apply inside their own groups, in either order.
s1, s2, then s3 and s4, then s5.

feedback.correct: Crowd, split, the two test rates, then the share of positives.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the crowd by the base rate before any test rate.

byKey.d1: The 10% applies to the 980 who are clear, not to everyone.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the 10% of 1,000 belongs.
byKey.s2: Split the crowd by the 2% before applying the test.
byKey.s5: The share of positives comes last, once both counts are known.
byKey.s1: Picture the crowd first, so every later count is whole.

explain.text: The crowd makes every count whole. Each test rate acts inside its own group, so the false positives are 10% of 980. The answer is a count over a count: 18 of 116.

screens.title: Sample spaces in code
screens.prose: `prob_dice(event, n_dice=2)` enumerates every roll of `n_dice` dice and returns the share for which `event(roll)` is true, as a `Fraction`. `natural_frequency(base, sens, fpr, n=1000)` takes rates as `Fraction`s. hints.text: In `natural_frequency`, `n * base` people have the condition.
True positives: that count times `sens`; false positives: the rest times `fpr`; then divide.

feedback.correct: Both functions count the sample space exactly.

screens.title: Drill: six at test pace
screens.prose: Six questions at the reported pace of about two minutes each: 12 minutes. Use your own watch; the app does not time you. Write the sample space first. Fractions in lowest terms or decimals to four places.
screens.question: Fill in each answer.

rows: Two dice: the total is prime
At least one head in four flips
Expected rolls of a die until the first 6
Two people born on the same day of the week
Two cards from a deck form a pair
Three flips all land the same way

hints.text: No head in four flips is $\tfrac{1}{16}$; a die needs 6 rolls on average for a 6.

feedback.correct: All six. Note your time against 12 minutes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows.

byKey.r2c1: A chance of $\tfrac16$ a roll takes 6 rolls on average.
byKey.r3c1: The first person fixes a day; the second matches it 1 time in 7.

explain.text: Each answer came from a sample space or a fixed first choice. The weekday and the pair both fix the first, then match. If you finished early, check only the rows you were unsure of.

screens.prose: A trader battery’s probability paper is reported as about 15 items in 30 minutes. A desk tests a signal over 100 days. Half are up days. It fires on 30% of up days and 10% of down days. Today it fired.
screens.question: What is the chance today is an up day?

options.why: That is the chance it fires on an up day. You want the reverse: up, given it fired.
That ignores the signal. 15 of the 20 firing days were up.
That is up and firing out of all 100 days. Divide by the 20 firing days instead.

hints.text: Up and firing: 15; down and firing: 5.

feedback.correct: 15 of the 20 firing days were up: $\tfrac34$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the firing days in each group, then take a share.

byKey.rev: That is the chance it fires on an up day. You want the reverse: up, given it fired.
byKey.base: That ignores the signal. 15 of the 20 firing days were up.
byKey.joint: That is up and firing out of all 100 days. Divide by the 20 firing days instead.

explain.text: Of 50 up days, 15 fire; of 50 down days, 5 fire. So 15 of the 20 firing days were up: $\tfrac34$. A signal that fires three times as often on up days turns even odds into 3 to 1.

ideas: Write the sample space or a crowd of 1,000 first, then count.
Work in fractions and simplify before reading the options; cross out anything above 1 or below 0.
Without replacement the second chance changes: two aces is $\tfrac{4}{52} \times \tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{221}$.

formula.name: Counting and multiplying
formula.note: A pair: the first card is free, then $\tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{17}$.

summary.trap: Using $\tfrac{4}{52}$ for the second card forgets that the first one left the deck.

quiz.question: What is the chance of at least one six?

options.why: You added $\tfrac16 + \tfrac16$, counting double six twice.
That is the chance of no six. Take it from 1.
That is a six on both dice. One is enough.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the grid cells with a six.

byKey.np: You added $\tfrac16 + \tfrac16$, counting double six twice.
byKey.comp: That is the chance of no six. Take it from 1.
byKey.both: That is a six on both dice. One is enough.

explain.text: A row of six and a column of six share one cell, so 11 cells have a six. That is $\tfrac{11}{36}$. Adding $\tfrac16$ twice counts the double six twice.

quiz.prose: An urn holds 3 red balls and 2 blue. Draw two without replacement.
quiz.question: What is the chance both are red?

options.why: You used $\tfrac35$ twice, as if the first ball went back.
That is one red ball. Both must be red.
The second draw is $\tfrac24$, but the first must be red too.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. After a red, 2 red remain among 4.

byKey.rep: You used $\tfrac35$ twice, as if the first ball went back.
byKey.one: That is one red ball. Both must be red.
byKey.half: The second draw is $\tfrac24$, but the first must be red too.

explain.text: First red: $\tfrac35$. Then 2 red among 4: $\tfrac24$. Multiply: $\tfrac{6}{20} = \tfrac{3}{10}$.

quiz.prose: 5% of emails are spam. A filter flags 80% of spam and 2% of genuine emails.
quiz.question: An email is flagged. What is the chance it is spam?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture 1,000 emails and count the flagged ones.

byKey.hit: 0.8 is flagged given spam. You want spam given flagged: 40 of 59.
byKey.joint: 0.04 is spam and flagged out of all 1,000. Divide by the 59 flagged.

explain.text: Of 1,000 emails, 50 are spam and 40 of them are flagged. Of 950 genuine, 19 are flagged. So 40 of 59 flagged emails are spam: 0.678.

quiz.prose: A question’s options are A $\tfrac75$, B $\tfrac23$, C $\tfrac13$ and D 0.4.
quiz.question: Which option can you cross out before reading the question?

options.why: $\tfrac23$ is a possible chance; it stays until you work.
$\tfrac13$ is a possible chance; it stays until you work.
0.4 is a possible chance; it stays until you work.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a value no probability can take.

byKey.b: $\tfrac23$ is a possible chance; it stays until you work.
byKey.c: $\tfrac13$ is a possible chance; it stays until you work.
byKey.d: 0.4 is a possible chance; it stays until you work.

explain.text: A probability lies between 0 and 1, and $\tfrac75 = 1.4$ does not. Crossing it out takes a second and leaves three. If the question asks for a probability, A is never the answer.
